terms.gloss: a picture cut into pieces: a jigsaw puzzle
terms.grammar: pictūra, pictūrae f., with the participle of dissecō; a piece is pars, partis f.
terms.comment: A description of ours: a picture (pictūra) cut up into pieces (dissecta, from dissecō, to cut in pieces, chiefly the elder Pliny’s word). We have found no word for a jigsaw puzzle in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, Levi–Bini, or Lewis & Short; Traupman’s aenigma is a puzzle in the sense of a riddle (see “riddle”). The pieces are simply partēs; of a piece that fits, convenit.

terms.gloss: fit (of a piece that goes into its place)
terms.grammar: in + acc., or with hūc: haec pars hūc convenit; nōn convenit, it doesn’t fit
evidence: Cato Agr. 21: fistulam ferream inditō, quae in columellam conveniat et in cūpam
Cic. Fin. 3.46: ad pedem aptē convenīre
terms.comment: Of one thing that fits into or onto another (Lewis & Short, sense II.B.1): Cato’s iron pipe that fits onto the post and into the hub, Cicero’s boot that fits the foot. So the plain word for a piece that fits. For “it doesn’t fit” in the sense “it doesn’t make sense”, see “it doesn’t add up”.

phrases.english: It doesn’t fit; look for another one.

phrases.latin: Eō fistulam ferream inditō, quae in columellam conveniat et in cūpam.
phrases.english: Put in an iron pipe there, to fit onto the post and into the hub.

phrases.latin: ut, sī cothurnī laus illa esset, ad pedem aptē convenīre
phrases.english: as if the whole merit of a boot were to fit the foot well

sources: Lewis & Short: pictura · Lewis & Short: disseco · Lewis & Short: convenio
